---
title: "Session 2: Importing and exporting data"
subtitle: "CSV, Excel, awkward files, and data straight from the World Bank"
---

::: {.objectifs}
Session objectives

- Locate files with `here::here()` instead of `setwd()`.
- Import CSV and Excel files, and inspect what you imported.
- Handle a badly formatted file: look at the raw text first, then check `nrow()` and `problems()`.
- Convert text to numbers (`parse_number()`), keep codes as text, tidy labels, and find the missing values a conversion created.
- Optional: clean country labels and parse dates with `lubridate`, then find the dates that failed.
- Export results to `output/` (CSV, Excel, `.rds`) without touching the raw data.
- Get World Bank data with the `WDI` package, and understand why we cache it.
:::

::: {.prepare}
Prepare your R session

**Packages used today:** `tidyverse`, `here`, `janitor`, `readxl`, `writexl`, `lubridate`, `scales`, `WDI`. If one is missing, run `install.packages("name")` in the console.

```{r}
#| label: setup
Sys.setenv(LANGUAGE = "en")   # R messages in English
library(tidyverse)   # readr, dplyr, ggplot2, ...
library(here)        # project-relative paths
library(janitor)     # clean_names()
library(readxl)      # read Excel files
library(writexl)     # write Excel files
library(lubridate)   # dates
library(scales)      # label_dollar()
library(WDI)         # World Bank API (used in a non-evaluated chunk)

source(here("R", "theme_cours.R"))
```

**Script of this session:** [download seance-2.R](../scripts/seance-2.R){download="seance-2.R"}, all the code of this page in one file.
:::

**Pacing.** The core path takes about 190 minutes, exercises included. Parts marked **Optional: going further** (Section 6 on strings and dates, Section 9, and Exercises 2.4, 2.5 and 2.7) add about 45 minutes: do them if time allows, or at home.

## 1. Where are my files?

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 10 min]{.duration} After this section you can say where a file lives and point R to it without `setwd()`.
:::

Every analysis in this course follows the same pipeline: import the data, check it, clean it, save the result.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
    A[Raw file in data/raw] --> B[Import]
    B --> C[Check]
    C --> D[Clean]
    D --> E[Save in output]
```

Last session you worked in an RStudio project. The project folder is the **working directory**. Our layout:

```
r-course/
├── r-course.Rproj
├── data/          # data given to you (from data.zip)
│   └── raw/       # original files, READ-ONLY
├── R/
│   └── theme_cours.R   # shared chart theme (from data.zip)
└── output/        # everything YOU produce (tables, exports)
```

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
    P[r-course/] --> D[data/]
    P --> R[R/]
    P --> O[output/]
    D --> RAW[data/raw/ read-only]
```

Rule: **never write into `data/`**. If you overwrite a raw file, the original is gone. Everything you create goes to `output/`.

Do not use `setwd("C:/Users/me/...")`. It breaks on every other computer. Use `here::here()`: it builds a path from the project root, whatever the machine.

```{r}
# here("data", "raw", "SCIM.csv") returns the full path on your machine,
# e.g. "/home/you/r-course/data/raw/SCIM.csv" (not printed here)
file.exists(here("data", "raw", "SCIM.csv"))
```

`file.exists()` returning `TRUE` is the first check to make when an import fails.

::: {.callout-note}
## In plain words

A path is an address. `setwd("C:/Users/me/...")` is like giving your home address to someone who lives elsewhere. `here()` gives directions *from the project's front door*, so the same directions work on every computer.
:::

## 2. CSV files with `readr`

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 30 min]{.duration} After this section you can read a CSV file and tell at a glance whether R understood it.
:::

A CSV (comma-separated values) file is plain text: one row per line, values separated by a delimiter. `read_csv()` guesses the type of each column from the first 1000 rows.

We use `SCIM.csv`, OECD data on international trade (exports, imports, trade balance) by country and period.

```{r}
scim <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "SCIM.csv"))
```

When you run this in the console, `readr` prints the number of rows and columns and the type it guessed for each: read it, it is the cheapest check you have (this page hides such messages). Now look at the data.

```{r}
head(scim)
glimpse(scim)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea

An import that runs without an error is **not** an import that worked. Always look at the result (`glimpse()`, `nrow()`) before using it.
:::

`glimpse()` shows every column on one line with its type: use it more than `head()`. `summary()` gives numeric summaries:

```{r}
summary(scim$Value)
```

**This summary is meaningless**, and R gives no warning: `Value` mixes US dollars, national currencies and percentage changes, some monthly and some quarterly. The maximum, 1,167,777, is Indonesia's quarterly trade in billions of rupiah. We check this below with `count()`.

What do we notice?

- Column names mix cases and contain spaces (`"Unit Code"`, `"Reference Period"`). Awkward to type, because you need backticks.
- Columns come in **French/English pairs** (`SUBJECT`/`Sujet`, `LOCATION`/`Pays`, `MEASURE`/`Mesure`, `TIME`/`Temps`): the same information twice.
- `TIME` is a text column that mixes months (`"2022-04"`) and quarters (`"2022-Q2"`).

`janitor::clean_names()` turns names into consistent `snake_case`:

```{r}
scim <- clean_names(scim)
names(scim)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Preview: dplyr verbs

`select()`, `filter()`, `count()`, `distinct()`, `mutate()`, `slice_max()` and `summarise()` are taught in Session 3 (ggplot in Session 5). For now, copy the pattern.
:::

Let us drop the French duplicates and the columns we do not need, but keep `unit_code` and `frequency`, then count what is left:

```{r}
scim <- scim |>
  select(subject, location, measure, frequency, time, unit_code, value)

scim |> count(subject)
scim |> count(measure, unit_code, frequency)
```

The three subjects are exports (`XTEXVA01`), imports (`XTIMVA01`) and net trade (`XTNTVA01`). The second count shows why we kept `unit_code` and `frequency`: `CXML` and `CXMLSA` are in US dollars, `NCML` and `NCMLSA` in national currency, `GPSA` and `GYSA` are percentage changes (from the previous period and from a year earlier), and each comes monthly (`M`) and quarterly (`Q`). Before computing anything on `value`, keep one measure and one frequency.

**Teaser: dates.** `time` is text, so R cannot sort or plot it as a date. `lubridate::yq()` converts `"2022-Q2"` to the first day of that quarter (the [Dates and times](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/datetimes.html) chapter of *R for Data Science* goes further, and so does [Section 6](#sec-strings-dates)):

```{r}
scim |>
  filter(str_detect(time, "Q")) |>
  distinct(time) |>
  mutate(date = yq(time))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

Opening a CSV in Excel and saving it back can **turn codes into dates** (the gene `SEPT2` becomes "2-Sep", the code `1-3` becomes a date) or change the **decimal mark**: in a French-language Excel, `3,5` means 3.5, but `read_csv()` expects a point. Check with `glimpse()`: a numeric column read as `<chr>` is the usual symptom. Fix it at the source or with `read_csv2()` (semicolon separator, decimal comma). Accented characters turned into `Ã©` signal a wrong **encoding**: add `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` (or `"UTF-8"`).
:::

## 3. Excel files with `readxl`

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 20 min]{.duration} After this section you can list the sheets of a workbook and read one sheet, or part of it.
:::

`read_excel()` reads `.xls` and `.xlsx` files. An Excel file can contain several **sheets**, so first list them:

```{r}
path_xlsx <- here("data", "raw", "SCIM.xlsx")
excel_sheets(path_xlsx)
```

Two sheets. By default `read_excel()` reads the first one. Choose a sheet by name or position with `sheet =`. Files made with French-language Excel often have French sheet names (`Feuil1`, `Feuil2`) and column names with accents or dashes (`Août-2022`); R needs backticks around such names.

```{r}
scim_xlsx <- read_excel(path_xlsx, sheet = "Sheet1")
dim(scim_xlsx)
scim_xlsx[1:5, 1:6]
```

This file is not the same as the CSV: it is in **wide format** (one column per month, one row per country), and the month names are in French. And the second sheet?

```{r}
dim(read_excel(path_xlsx, sheet = "Feuil2"))
```

It is empty (0 rows, 0 columns); `Feuil2` is the French default name for "Sheet 2". Lesson: do not assume what a sheet contains.

To read only part of a sheet, use `range =` (Excel notation):

```{r}
read_excel(path_xlsx, sheet = "Sheet1", range = "A1:D6")
```

## 4. A hard import: the WID file

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 35 min]{.duration} After this section you can import a malformed file and prove, with numbers, that the import is right.
:::

Real files are rarely clean. `WID_Data.csv` comes from the [World Inequality Database](https://wid.world): Gini coefficients of pre-tax national income for China, India and the USA. Before running any code, **look at the raw text**:

```{r}
readLines(here("data", "raw", "WID_Data.csv"), n = 9)
```

Three problems:

1. The first line is a **comment** ("Downloaded from wid.world..."), not a header.
2. Separator is `;`, not `,`.
3. The variable label is **spread over several lines** inside quotes, and there is no header row.

A naive `read_csv()` does not fail loudly. It returns something:

```{r}
#| warning: false
wid_naive <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "WID_Data.csv"))   # naive attempt
dim(wid_naive)
head(wid_naive, 3)
```

One column, 190 "rows" that are fragments of text, and the comment line became the column name. We know the file has 3 countries × 21 years = 63 observations, so 190 is wrong. `problems()` lists the cells `readr` could not parse; here it flags only one, so it is not enough: **your own `nrow()` check is what catches the error**.

```{r}
problems(wid_naive) |> select(-file)   # hide the long path
```

::: {.callout-note}
## In plain words

`read_csv()` is a tourist with a phrasebook for one language only. Faced with a file whose "grammar" is different (`;` separator, a comment on line 1), it does not stop: it invents a reading. You are the interpreter: look at the raw text, then tell `readr` the rules.
:::

Now read it properly: skip the comment line, say the delimiter is `;`, and provide the column names ourselves.

```{r}
wid <- read_delim(
  here("data", "raw", "WID_Data.csv"),
  delim = ";",
  skip = 1,                                   # the comment line
  col_names = c("country_wid", "indicator", "percentile", "year", "gini"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
nrow(wid)
glimpse(wid)
```

63 rows, as expected. Side by side, the naive result and the correct one:

```{r}
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| echo: false
print(wid_naive |> rename(comment_line_as_name = 1) |> head(4), width = 40)
print(wid |> select(country_wid, year, gini) |> head(4))
```

The multi-line label ends up in `indicator`: quoted text may contain line breaks, and `readr` handles that. Compare with the cleaned version `data/wid_gini.csv` prepared for this course:

```{r}
wid_gini <- read_csv(here("data", "wid_gini.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(wid_gini)

# Same numbers? (the cleaned file has an iso3c code in addition)
all.equal(wid$gini, wid_gini$gini)
```

A chart is also a check: if the import is right, the series should look like inequality data, not like noise. This is the WID Gini index (0 = perfect equality, 1 = one person receives all the income) once imported correctly.

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the WID Gini index, 2000-2020, for China, India and the USA. All three rise. India overtakes the USA in 2007 and stays the highest from then on; its line is almost straight until 2011 and flat from 2014. The USA jumps in 2020."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(wid_gini, aes(x = year, y = gini, colour = iso3c)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(CHN = pal_cours[["accent"]],
                                 IND = "#E69F00",
                                 USA = pal_cours[["principal"]])) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Income inequality rose in China, India and the USA, 2000-2020", 60),
    x = NULL, y = "Gini index (0-1)", colour = NULL,
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Inequality Database (WID), pre-tax national income.", 95)
  )
```

Read the chart as a check, not only as a result. India's line is almost straight from 2000 to 2011 (about +0.01 every year), then perfectly flat from 2014 to 2020 (0.634 every year): these are WID interpolations, not yearly measurements, because India has few surveys. The US jump in 2020 (0.58 to 0.62) also deserves a look. Check the WID metadata before reading year-to-year changes.

::: {.callout-important}
## The checklist for any new file

1. Open the raw text (`readLines(path, n = 10)`) before reading it.
2. After the import: `nrow()`, `ncol()`, `glimpse()`: do they match what you expect?
3. `problems(x)` lists the cells `readr` could not parse.
4. Check missing values and types (`summary()`).
:::

The cleaned file carries an `iso3c` code (country code). Notice that WID writes `"USA"` where the World Bank writes `"United States"`: country names differ between sources. We will see in session 3 why you must join on codes, never on names.

## 5. Converting and cleaning values {#sec-convert}

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 20 min]{.duration} After this section you can turn text into numbers, keep codes as text, tidy labels, and find the values a conversion lost.
:::

`glimpse()` tells you that a column has the wrong type. This section is about **fixing** it, and checking the fix. We use `repair_me.csv`: real World Bank values for six countries in 2015 and 2019, with problems planted on purpose. You will repair it completely in Session 3; here we practise one fix at a time.

```{r}
repair <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "repair_me.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(repair)
```

Read the types. `gdp_pc_ppp` is `<dbl>`: `readr` understood that `"2,967.7"` is a number with a thousands separator. `iso_num` is `<chr>` and keeps `"004"`. But `life_exp` is `<chr>`: at least one value in it is not a number. We come back to it at the end.

### Numbers stored as text

Not every tool is as helpful as `readr`. Base R's `read.csv()`, which you will meet in many answers online, reads the same file differently:

```{r}
repair_base <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "repair_me.csv"))
str(repair_base)
```

`gdp_pc_ppp` is now text (`chr`). The reflex `as.numeric()` fails on every value, because of the comma:

```{r}
#| warning: true
as.numeric(repair_base$gdp_pc_ppp)
```

Thirteen `NA` and one warning: `NAs introduced by coercion`. `readr::parse_number()` drops the thousands separator, and any text around the number:

```{r}
parse_number(repair_base$gdp_pc_ppp)
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

`parse_number()` keeps the first number it finds and drops everything else: `"12 km"` and `"12 miles"` both become `12`. Look at the text before you convert it. For French-style numbers (`"2.967,7"` or `"2 967,7"`), tell it which mark is which with `locale =`:

```{r}
parse_number("12 km")
parse_number("2.967,7", locale = locale(decimal_mark = ",", grouping_mark = "."))
```
:::

### Codes that must stay text

`iso_num` is the ISO numeric country code: Afghanistan is `"004"`. A code is a label, not a quantity: you never add two codes, but you join tables on them. `read.csv()` turned it into a number, and the zeros are gone:

```{r}
repair_base$iso_num
```

`4` will never match `"004"` in another file. With `readr`, declare the type instead of trusting the guess:

```{r}
repair_codes <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "repair_me.csv"),
                         col_types = cols(iso_num = col_character()))
repair_codes$iso_num
```

Here the guess was already right (the version of `readr` used for this page keeps values with leading zeros as text), but a guess depends on the version and on the first 1000 rows. `col_types =` writes the rule down: the same script gives the same result on every computer.

### Spaces and case in labels

`read_csv()` silently removes spaces at the ends of each value (its argument `trim_ws = TRUE`); `read.csv()` keeps them. `unique()` prints each value in quotes, so you can see them:

```{r}
unique(repair$country)        # read_csv(): spaces removed, case problem left
unique(repair_base$country)   # read.csv(): both problems
```

For R, `" kenya"` and `"KENYA "` are two different countries, and neither is `"Kenya"`. `str_squish()` removes spaces at both ends (and doubled spaces inside); `str_to_title()` puts a capital at the start of each word:

```{r}
str_squish(c(" kenya", "KENYA ", "Burkina   Faso"))
unique(str_to_title(str_squish(repair_base$country)))
```

Six names for six countries. (We only print the result: the table itself is repaired in Session 3.)

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

Running `str_to_title()` on names that were already right. It does not know country names:

```{r}
str_to_title(c("Côte d'Ivoire", "United States of America"))
```

Check with `unique()` after every cleaning step, and fix the exceptions one by one ([Section 6](#sec-strings-dates) shows how). Better still, match countries on codes, not on names.
:::

### Missing values created by a conversion

Back to `life_exp`. Count the missing values before and after converting:

```{r}
#| warning: true
sum(is.na(repair$life_exp))   # before
life_num <- as.numeric(repair$life_exp)
sum(is.na(life_num))          # after
```

One `NA` appeared that was not in the file. To find it, keep the rows where the text was present but the number is missing:

```{r}
repair |>
  mutate(life_num = as.numeric(life_exp)) |>
  filter(!is.na(life_exp), is.na(life_num)) |>
  select(country, year, life_exp, life_num)
```

Benin 2015 is written `"n/a"`. Now **decide**. If it were a typo (`"6l.2"`), you would look up the right value at the source. Here `"n/a"` is the provider's way to write "missing", so declare it at import with `na =`:

```{r}
repair_na <- read_csv(here("data", "raw", "repair_me.csv"),
                      na = c("", "NA", "n/a"), show_col_types = FALSE)
class(repair_na$life_exp)
sum(is.na(repair_na$life_exp))
```

`life_exp` is now numeric, with one `NA` that we chose. `na =` replaces the default `c("", "NA")`, so keep those two in the list.

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea

A conversion can turn a value into `NA` with only a warning, or with none at all. Count `NA` before and after every conversion: each new `NA` must have an explanation.
:::

The file still has a problem we have not touched; Session 3's "Repair this analysis" exercise puts all the fixes together. Practise now with Exercise 2.6.

## 6. Strings and dates: a small worked example (Optional: going further) {#sec-strings-dates}

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 20 min]{.duration} After this section you can harmonise country labels, turn date text into real dates, and find the dates that failed.
:::

This section is not needed for the next sessions: do it if you finish early, or at home. Annual WDI data have no dates, but survey data do. Here is a small table of household interviews, typed by different enumerators:

```{r}
interviews <- tibble(
  country   = c("Senegal", "senegal ", "Côte d'Ivoire", "Cote d'Ivoire", "IVORY COAST", " Ghana"),
  interview = c("15/03/2019", "02/11/2019", "30/06/2020", "31/02/2020", "14/07/2020", "03/12/2019")
)
interviews
```

**Labels.** First the two steps of [Section 5](#sec-convert), spaces then case. Then one `case_when()` (taught in Session 3: read it as "if ... then ...") gathers the variant names, including the one `str_to_title()` damaged:

```{r}
interviews <- interviews |>
  mutate(
    country = str_to_title(str_squish(country)),
    country = case_when(
      country %in% c("Côte D'ivoire", "Cote D'ivoire", "Ivory Coast") ~ "Côte d'Ivoire",
      .default = country   # every other label stays as it is
    )
  )
count(interviews, country)
```

Three countries, as expected.

**Dates.** In Section 2, `yq()` turned `"2022-Q2"` into a date. Every `lubridate` parser is named after the order of the parts in the text: `y` year, `m` month, `d` day, `q` quarter.

```{r}
ymd("2019-03-15")
dmy("15/03/2019")
my("03/2019")
yq("2019-Q1")
```

All four return a `Date`. Our interviews are written day/month/year, so we use `dmy()`, then extract the year with `year()`:

```{r}
#| warning: true
interviews <- interviews |>
  mutate(date = dmy(interview), year = year(date))
interviews
```

The warning `1 failed to parse` means that one text could not be read as a date. As in Section 5, find it with `is.na()`:

```{r}
interviews |> filter(is.na(date))
```

The 31st of February does not exist: an entry error. Do not guess the right day; ask the source (questionnaire, survey team), or keep the `NA` and say so.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

`"02/11/2019"` is 2 November with `dmy()` but 11 February with `mdy()`, and both run **without any warning**. `lubridate` cannot know which convention the source used: read its documentation (US sources often put the month first), and check that `range(interviews$date, na.rm = TRUE)` falls inside the fieldwork period.
:::

Practise with Exercise 2.7 (optional).

## 7. Writing files

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can save a result in the format that suits its reader.
:::

Create the `output/` folder (nothing happens if it already exists), then write there.

```{r}
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
```

**Text files.** `write_csv()` writes a comma-separated file, `write_delim()` any delimiter:

```{r}
write_csv(wid_gini, here("output", "wid_gini_copy.csv"))
write_delim(wid_gini, here("output", "wid_gini_tab.txt"), delim = "\t")
```

**Excel.** `writexl::write_xlsx()` writes one sheet from a data frame, or **several sheets from a named list**; the names become the sheet names:

```{r}
write_xlsx(wid_gini, here("output", "wid_gini.xlsx"))

write_xlsx(
  list(wid_clean = wid_gini, scim_sample = head(scim, 100)),
  here("output", "two_sheets.xlsx")
)
excel_sheets(here("output", "two_sheets.xlsx"))
```

**R's own format: `.rds`.** A CSV loses information (column types, factor levels). `saveRDS()` stores one R object exactly as it is; `readRDS()` restores it.

```{r}
saveRDS(wid_gini, here("output", "wid_gini.rds"))
wid_back <- readRDS(here("output", "wid_gini.rds"))
all.equal(wid_gini, wid_back)   # TRUE: same values, types and names
```

::: {.callout-important}
## Key idea

Your raw data never changes; your outputs can always be regenerated by re-running the script. If you can delete `output/` and rebuild it, your work is **reproducible**.
:::

When to use what?

| Format | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `.csv` | sharing with others or other software; the file must be readable anywhere |
| `.xlsx` | the recipient works in Excel (several tables in one file) |
| `.rds` | you want to reload the object in R exactly as it was (intermediate results) |

## 8. Data from packages: the World Bank

::: {.section-goal}
[≈ 25 min]{.duration} After this section you can fetch World Bank data with `WDI()` and explain why we read a cached copy.
:::

Many institutions provide an R package to fetch their data directly. The `WDI` package queries the World Bank's **World Development Indicators**. Each indicator has a code, e.g. `NY.GDP.MKTP.CD` = GDP in current US dollars. Find a code with `WDIsearch()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
WDIsearch("gdp per capita")      # needs Internet
```

Fetching GDP for the USA, China and India looks like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
gdp_api <- WDI(
  country   = c("US", "CN", "IN"),     # ISO-2 codes
  indicator = c(gdp = "NY.GDP.MKTP.CD"),  # new_name = indicator code
  start = 2000, end = 2020
)
```

This chunk is **not evaluated** when this page is built: it needs an Internet connection and the World Bank server may be slow or change its data. Instead, the course uses a **cached copy** saved once by `R/00_prepare_data.R`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why cache data?

- **Reproducibility**: the World Bank revises its series. Today's call may give different numbers than last year's.
- **Robustness**: no Internet, no download, no failure. Your classroom Wi-Fi is not a dependency.
- **Speed**: calling an API at every run is slow.

Good practice: fetch once, save the file in your project, read the file afterwards, and note the download date.
:::

```{r}
wdi3 <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_3countries.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(wdi3)
```

We also have a larger **panel**: all countries, 2000–2023, six indicators. It will be our main dataset from session 3.

```{r}
wdi_panel <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
glimpse(wdi_panel)
```

Before using a panel, ask: **how much of it is actually observed?** The chart below shows, for each indicator and year, the share of countries with a non-missing value. (Lines near 100% overlap: `population` and `life_exp` are fully observed.)

```{r}
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of the share of countries with a non-missing value, by indicator and year, 2000-2023. Most indicators sit near 100%; the Gini index is clearly lower."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the chart code (taught in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
wdi_panel |>
  summarise(across(c(gdp, gdp_pc_ppp, population, life_exp, gini, elec_access),
                   \(x) mean(!is.na(x))),
            .by = year) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "indicator", values_to = "share_observed") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = share_observed, colour = indicator)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = str_wrap("Most indicators cover nearly all countries; the Gini index does not", 60),
    x = NULL, y = "Share of countries with a value", colour = NULL,
    caption = str_wrap("Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2000-2023.", 95)
  )
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common mistake

Averaging or comparing an indicator without checking its coverage. If the Gini index is observed for under half of the countries in a year, any "world average" describes a **selected group** (countries that run household surveys), not the world.
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Why it matters for development economics

Missing data in WDI is not random: low-income and fragile countries are the ones with the fewest observations. Checking coverage first tells you whom your results are about.
:::

## Exercise 2.4 (Optional: going further)

Write the `WDI()` call that would fetch total population (`SP.POP.TOTL`) for Japan, Germany and Brazil from 2000 to 2020. (You cannot run it in class without Internet: write it only.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| eval: false
pop_api <- WDI(
  country   = c("JP", "DE", "BR"),
  indicator = c(population = "SP.POP.TOTL"),
  start = 2000, end = 2020
)
# then save it once, so that you never have to call the API again:
dir.create(here("output"), showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(pop_api, here("output", "pop_3countries.csv"))
```
`WDI()` takes ISO-2 country codes (or `"all"`), a named vector of indicators (`new_name = code`) and a period. The result has one row per country-year.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 2.6: from text to numbers

Someone typed these amounts by hand:

```{r}
x <- c(" 12", "1,200", "n/a", "7 ")
```

1. Run `as.numeric(x)`. How many `NA` do you get? Which one is a real missing value, and which one is a conversion failure?
2. Convert `x` with `parse_number()`. Which value is now right?
3. Tell `parse_number()` that `"n/a"` means missing (argument `na =`). Check with `sum(is.na())` that exactly one `NA` remains, and that the warning has gone.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| warning: true
as.numeric(x)                             # spaces are fine; the comma and "n/a" are not
sum(is.na(as.numeric(x)))
parse_number(x)                           # 1200 is right; "n/a" still gives a warning
parse_number(x, na = "n/a")               # "n/a" declared missing: no warning
sum(is.na(parse_number(x, na = "n/a")))
```
`as.numeric()` gives two `NA`: `"n/a"` is a real missing value, `"1,200"` is a conversion failure. `parse_number()` reads `"1,200"` as 1200. Once `"n/a"` is declared with `na =`, the only `NA` left is the one you expected.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 2.7 (Optional: going further)

Field visits, one row per visit, with the month typed as month/year:

```{r}
visits <- tibble(
  country = c("Gambia, The", "the  gambia", "THE GAMBIA ", "Senegal", "senegal"),
  month   = c("03/2018", "11/2018", "13/2019", "06/2019", "09/2019")
)
```

1. Clean `country` so that there are exactly two names, `"The Gambia"` and `"Senegal"`.
2. Turn `month` into a date with the right `lubridate` function. Which row fails, and why?
3. Add the year and count the visits by country and year.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Show solution
```{r}
#| warning: true
visits <- visits |>
  mutate(
    country = str_to_title(str_squish(country)),
    country = case_when(country == "Gambia, The" ~ "The Gambia",   # World Bank spelling
                        .default = country),
    date = my(month),
    year = year(date)
  )
visits |> filter(is.na(date))   # month 13 does not exist
visits |> count(country, year)
```
`my()` reads month then year. `"13/2019"` fails to parse: there is no 13th month. Its year is `NA` too, so the count shows one visit to The Gambia with an unknown year: report it, do not drop it silently.
:::

## Key takeaways

- Never use `setwd()` or absolute paths: `here::here()` works on every machine.
- `data/raw/` is read-only. Everything you produce goes to `output/`.
- Look at the raw text of a file before reading it, and check `nrow()`, `glimpse()` and `problems()` after.
- `read_csv()` for commas, `read_delim()` for other separators (`skip =`, `col_names =`); `read_excel()` with `sheet =` and `range =`.
- `clean_names()` makes column names usable; duplicated columns and text dates are common in real data.
- Numbers stored as text: `parse_number()`, not `as.numeric()`. Codes stay text: `col_types = cols(code = col_character())`. Labels: `str_squish()`, then check with `unique()`.
- Count `NA` before and after every conversion; declare the provider's missing codes at import with `na = c("", "NA", "n/a")`.
- Dates: the `lubridate` function follows the order in the text (`dmy()`, `ymd()`, `my()`, `yq()`); a `failed to parse` warning means `NA` to find with `is.na()`.
- Write with `write_csv()`, `write_xlsx()` (a named list gives several sheets) and `saveRDS()` to keep R objects exactly.
- Cache API data (`WDI`) in a file: reproducible, offline, fast.
